questions.question: In scaled dot-product attention, why are the dot products of queries and keys divided by the square root of the key dimension (d_k)?
options: To stop large dot products from saturating softmax and shrinking its gradients
To reduce the memory needed to store the attention matrix
To make attention cost grow linearly with sequence length
To make the attention weights in each row add up to exactly one before the softmax
questions.explanation: For large d_k the dot products grow in magnitude, so softmax saturates and its gradients become extremely small. Scaling by 1/sqrt(d_k) counteracts this. The softmax itself makes the weights sum to one, and the scaling changes neither memory nor the quadratic cost.

source.title: Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (Sec. 3.2.1)

questions.question: What is the main benefit of multi-head attention compared with a single attention head of the same total dimension?
options: It removes the need for positional encodings in the input
It processes tokens one after another, like a recurrent network
It needs far fewer parameters than a single wide attention head
Heads can attend to different representation subspaces at once
questions.explanation: Multi-head attention projects queries, keys and values several times with different learned projections, so different heads can capture different relationships (e.g. syntax vs. coreference). It does not replace positional encodings and the parameter count is about the same as a single full-width head.

source.title: Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (Sec. 3.2.2)

questions.question: A Transformer has no recurrence and no convolution. How does the original architecture give the model information about token order?
options: The vocabulary contains separate tokens for each position
Positional encodings are added to the token embeddings
Tokens are processed one at a time, from left to right
A convolution over neighbouring tokens captures their order
questions.explanation: Self-attention is permutation-invariant, so the original Transformer adds sinusoidal positional encodings to the token embeddings. Later models use learned or rotary (RoPE) position embeddings, but the idea is the same: inject position information explicitly.

source.title: Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (Sec. 3.5)

questions.question: In an encoder-decoder Transformer used for translation, where do the decoder's cross-attention keys and values come from?
options: From the token embedding table of the source
From the output of the encoder stack
From a separate retrieval index of documents
From the decoder's own previous layer only
questions.explanation: In encoder-decoder (cross) attention the queries come from the previous decoder layer, while the keys and values come from the encoder output. This lets every decoder position attend over the whole source sentence.

source.title: Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (Sec. 3.2.3)

questions.question: Why does a GPT-style decoder apply a causal (look-ahead) mask in self-attention?
options: Padding tokens are ignored when batching inputs
Each position may only attend to earlier positions
The attention matrix becomes sparse and faster
The model can attend to future tokens at inference
questions.explanation: A causal mask blocks attention to future positions, so the prediction for token t depends only on tokens before t. This keeps the model autoregressive. Padding masks are a different mechanism.

source.title: Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (Sec. 3.2.3)

questions.question: A team needs to classify support tickets into categories and extract named entities. They want a model that sees context on both sides of every token. Which architecture fits best?
options: A diffusion model with a text encoder
An encoder-only model such as BERT
A recurrent model without any attention
A decoder-only model such as GPT
questions.explanation: Encoder-only models like BERT are bidirectional: each token's representation is conditioned on left and right context, which suits classification and token-level tasks such as NER. Decoder-only models are optimized for generation with left-to-right context.

source.title: Devlin et al., BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers

questions.question: What is the pre-training objective that lets BERT learn bidirectional representations?
options: Predicting randomly masked tokens from both sides of context
Matching images with captions using a contrastive loss
Reconstructing images after Gaussian noise is added
Predicting the next token using only the previous tokens of the text
questions.explanation: BERT masks about 15% of input tokens and predicts them using both left and right context (MLM). It also used next sentence prediction. Causal LM is the GPT objective and would only give left context.

source.title: Devlin et al., BERT (Sec. 3.1, Masked LM)

questions.question: Which two tasks are a natural fit for an encoder-decoder (sequence-to-sequence) model such as T5? (Select two.)
options: Machine translation
Approximate nearest-neighbour search over vectors
Computing an image's pixel histogram
Sorting a list of numbers in a database
Abstractive summarization
questions.explanation: Encoder-decoder models map an input sequence to a different output sequence, which is exactly translation and summarization. T5 frames all NLP tasks as text-to-text. The other options are not sequence generation tasks.

source.title: Raffel et al., Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning (T5)

questions.question: Self-attention over a sequence of n tokens has what time and memory complexity with respect to n in the standard Transformer?
options: Linear, O(n)
Linearithmic, O(n log n)
Logarithmic, O(log n)
Quadratic, O(n^2)
questions.explanation: Every token attends to every other token, so the attention score matrix is n x n. This quadratic cost is why long context windows are expensive and why techniques like FlashAttention and sparse attention exist.

source.title: Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (Table 1)

questions.question: Which two reasons explain why Transformers train faster than RNNs on modern GPUs? (Select two.)
options: They have far fewer parameters than any recurrent network of similar quality
Their work is dominated by large matrix multiplications that GPUs accelerate well
They skip backpropagation and learn with a single forward pass per batch
They only work on sequences shorter than 512 tokens, which fit in cache
All positions of a sequence are processed in parallel, not step by step
questions.explanation: RNNs must compute hidden states one step after another. Transformers compute all positions at once with attention and feed-forward layers, which are big matrix multiplications that map well to GPU cores and Tensor Cores. They still train with backpropagation and are usually larger, not smaller.

source.title: Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (Abstract)

questions.question: Which two components are found in every layer of the original Transformer encoder? (Select two.)
options: A convolutional layer with max pooling over neighbouring tokens
An LSTM cell that carries a hidden state across positions
A multi-head self-attention sub-layer
A position-wise feed-forward network
A k-means clustering step that groups similar tokens
questions.explanation: Each encoder layer has two sub-layers: multi-head self-attention and a position-wise fully connected feed-forward network, each wrapped with a residual connection and layer normalization. There is no convolution or recurrence.

source.title: Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (Sec. 3.1)

questions.question: Why do modern LLMs use subword tokenization (e.g. BPE) rather than whole-word vocabularies? (Select two.)
options: It guarantees exactly one token per character
The vocabulary stays a manageable, fixed size
It makes every language use the same number of tokens
It removes the need for an embedding layer
Rare or unseen words can still be split into known pieces
questions.explanation: Subword methods keep frequent words whole and split rare words into smaller known units, so there are almost no out-of-vocabulary words while the vocabulary stays a fixed, manageable size. Character-level tokenization would make sequences much longer, and token counts still differ between languages.

source.title: Hugging Face Transformers, Summary of the tokenizers

questions.question: How does Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) build its vocabulary during training?
options: Assigns exactly one token to every word seen in the corpus
Starts large and removes the tokens that least reduce likelihood
Starts from characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent pair
Clusters word embeddings with k-means into token groups
questions.explanation: BPE begins with a base vocabulary of characters (or bytes) and iteratively merges the most frequent pair until it reaches the target vocabulary size. Removing tokens from a large starting vocabulary describes the Unigram method.

source.title: Hugging Face LLM Course, Byte-Pair Encoding tokenization

questions.question: Which tokenization algorithm was used by the original BERT model?
options: WordPiece
Unigram with SentencePiece
Whitespace splitting
Byte-level BPE
questions.explanation: BERT uses WordPiece, which marks word-internal pieces with the ## prefix (e.g. 'token', '##ization'). GPT-2 uses byte-level BPE, and models such as T5 use Unigram via SentencePiece.

source.title: Hugging Face LLM Course, WordPiece tokenization

questions.question: A developer pastes the same paragraph in English and in Portuguese into an English-centric LLM and sees that the Portuguese version uses many more tokens. What is the most likely cause?
options: The tokenizer was trained mostly on English text
The model counts each accent as a separate sentence
Token counts increase when the temperature is higher
Portuguese words always have more letters than English
questions.explanation: A tokenizer learns merges from its training corpus. Languages under-represented in that corpus get fewer whole-word tokens and are split into more pieces, which increases cost and uses more of the context window.

source.title: Hugging Face LLM Course, Chapter 6: The Tokenizers library

questions.question: What is a key property of SentencePiece compared with tokenizers that require pre-tokenization on spaces?
options: It works on raw text and treats spaces as a normal symbol
It produces exactly one token per byte without any merges
It needs a separate dictionary of whole words to work
It can only tokenize English and other space-separated text
questions.explanation: SentencePiece operates on raw text, treating whitespace as a normal symbol (shown as ▁). This makes it language-independent and suitable for languages like Japanese or Chinese that don't separate words with spaces.

source.title: Kudo & Richardson, SentencePiece

questions.question: What does a token embedding layer in an LLM do?
options: Maps each token ID to a learned dense vector
Splits the raw input text into tokens
Converts output vectors back into readable text
Stores the conversation history between turns
questions.explanation: The embedding layer is a lookup table from token IDs to learned dense vectors that the Transformer layers process. Splitting text into tokens is the tokenizer's job, which happens before the embedding layer.

source.title: Dive into Deep Learning, Attention Mechanisms and Transformers

questions.question: A model's answers are too repetitive and predictable for a creative writing app. Which single change is most likely to make outputs more varied?
options: Increase the sampling temperature
Switch to greedy decoding (argmax)
Reduce max_tokens
Lower top-p to 0.1 for safer picks
questions.explanation: Higher temperature flattens the probability distribution, so less likely tokens are sampled more often and outputs become more diverse. Greedy decoding and a very low top-p both make output more deterministic, and max_tokens only limits length.

source.title: Prompt Engineering Guide, LLM Settings

questions.question: What does top-p (nucleus) sampling do?
options: Always picks the single most probable next token
Samples only from a fixed number k of the likeliest tokens at each step
Samples from the smallest token set whose probabilities reach p
Penalizes tokens that have already appeared in the output
questions.explanation: Nucleus sampling keeps the most likely tokens until their cumulative probability reaches p, then samples from that set, so the candidate set size adapts to the model's confidence. A fixed number of candidates is top-k; penalizing repeats is a repetition/frequency penalty.

source.title: Hugging Face, Generation strategies

questions.question: A data-extraction service must return the same JSON fields for the same input every time. Which decoding setting is most appropriate?
options: Temperature at or near 0
Top-k of 500
Temperature of 1.5
A high presence penalty
questions.explanation: With temperature near 0 the model almost always picks the most probable token, giving the most deterministic and factual outputs, which suits extraction and classification. High temperature or large top-k increase randomness.

source.title: Prompt Engineering Guide, LLM Settings

questions.question: How does beam search differ from greedy decoding?
options: It decodes from right to left instead of from left to right
It samples each token at random according to the temperature and top-p
It keeps several candidate sequences and returns the most probable one
It works only with encoder-only models such as BERT
questions.explanation: Greedy decoding takes the most likely token at each step. Beam search keeps the num_beams most likely partial sequences, so it can find a higher-probability full sequence that greedy would miss. It is deterministic, not random.

source.title: Hugging Face, Generation strategies

questions.question: A chatbot sometimes cuts answers off mid-sentence and sometimes keeps generating a fake 'User:' turn. Which two generation parameters address these problems? (Select two.)
options: Increase the number of attention heads
Lower the embedding dimension
Raise max_tokens (maximum new tokens)
Add a stop sequence such as 'User:'
Switch the tokenizer from BPE to WordPiece
questions.explanation: Cut-off answers usually mean the max_tokens limit was reached. Stop sequences end generation when a given string appears, which prevents the model from inventing the next turn. The other options are architecture choices, not generation settings.

source.title: Prompt Engineering Guide, LLM Settings

questions.question: What is an LLM's context window?
options: The maximum tokens (input plus output) handled in one request
How long a conversation stays in memory on the server
The number of documents the model can retrieve from its vector database
The number of epochs used to pre-train the model
questions.explanation: The context window is the maximum sequence length the model attends over, counting input and output tokens. Anything beyond it must be truncated, summarized or retrieved selectively.

source.title: NVIDIA Glossary, What is Generative AI?

questions.question: A RAG app puts the key passage in the middle of a very long prompt and accuracy drops. Moving it to the start or end fixes it. Which known behavior explains this?
options: Models ignore everything after the first 100 tokens of the prompt they receive
Temperature is applied more strongly to the middle of prompts
The tokenizer drops tokens from the middle of long inputs
Models use the start and end of long contexts better than the middle
questions.explanation: The 'lost in the middle' study found that performance is highest when relevant information is at the start or end of the input and degrades when it is in the middle of long contexts. This motivates reranking and putting the best chunks first.

source.title: Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts

questions.question: What is a foundation model?
options: A small model trained from scratch for exactly one narrow task
A rule-based system written by domain experts
A database that stores the weights of other models
A large model trained on broad data, adaptable to many tasks
questions.explanation: Foundation models are trained on large, broad datasets (often self-supervised) and then adapted, through prompting, fine-tuning or PEFT, to many tasks. GPT, Llama and Nemotron are examples.

source.title: NVIDIA Blog, What Are Foundation Models?

questions.question: Why can an LLM produce a fluent, confident answer that is factually wrong? (Select two.)
options: It generates statistically likely text rather than looking up verified facts
It only produces errors when the prompt is written in a language other than English
Its knowledge comes from training data that may be missing or out of date
It deliberately invents facts whenever the temperature is set above 0.5
Its tokenizer corrupts numbers and proper names in the generated output
questions.explanation: LLMs predict plausible next tokens from patterns in their training data. If the fact is missing, rare or outdated in that data they can still produce a confident 'hallucination'. RAG, citations, lower temperature and verification reduce this but don't eliminate it.

source.title: NVIDIA Blog, What Is Retrieval-Augmented Generation?

questions.question: According to the Chinchilla scaling study, for a fixed training compute budget, how should model size and training tokens be scaled?
options: Neither: for a fixed compute budget, only the learning rate schedule matters
Roughly equally: double the tokens when you double the model size
Mostly model size: data can stay fixed as the model grows
Mostly data: model size should stay fixed as data grows
questions.explanation: Hoffmann et al. found that many large models were undertrained and that, for compute-optimal training, parameters and training tokens should be scaled in equal proportion. Chinchilla (70B) trained on more tokens outperformed the larger Gopher (280B).

source.title: Hoffmann et al., Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models

questions.question: Which two statements about Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs are correct? (Select two.)
options: All experts must still be loaded in memory, even though few are used per token
It is a model that can only answer questions from domain experts
A router activates only a few experts per token, so compute per token is below the total size
Every token passes through all experts, so MoE is always slower than dense models
It combines separately trained chatbots by majority vote
questions.explanation: In a sparse MoE layer a gating network routes each token to a small subset of experts. Capacity (total parameters) grows without a proportional increase in compute per token, but all expert weights still have to fit in memory.

source.title: Shazeer et al., Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer

questions.question: Which two techniques are used inside Transformer layers to make deep stacks trainable? (Select two.)
options: Removing the softmax from attention
Max pooling between layers
Layer normalization
Residual (skip) connections around each sub-layer
Training each layer with a separate optimizer
questions.explanation: Each sub-layer is wrapped as LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)) in the original paper. Residual connections ease gradient flow and layer normalization stabilizes activations. Max pooling is a CNN technique.

source.title: Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (Sec. 3.1)

questions.question: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), used in models such as Llama, encodes position by:
options: Rotating queries and keys by a position-dependent angle
Training a separate model that predicts each position
Appending the position number as an extra input token
Sorting the attention matrix by token position
questions.explanation: RoPE multiplies queries and keys by position-dependent rotation matrices. The dot product between a rotated query and key then depends on their relative distance, which gives relative position information.

source.title: Su et al., RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding
